summary.text: A 27-year-old man with a 4-year history of idiopathic epilepsy, previously on levetiracetam, was referred to cardiology for recurrent syncopal episodes and an abnormal electrocardiogram. Syncope began after lamotrigine was introduced; ECGs before lamotrigine showed normal sinus rhythm without a type 1 Brugada pattern. His most recent admission was for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure terminated with intravenous lorazepam; a baseline emergency department ECG showed V1 and V2 ST elevation, a prominent J wave and negative T waves: a type 1 Brugada pattern.

Transthoracic echocardiography showed no structural heart disease, head CT showed no brain abnormalities and the awake EEG showed well-organized activity without spike-and-wave discharges or lateralizing abnormalities. Repeat ECGs were consistent with a type 1 Brugada pattern. A positive electrophysiological study with programmed stimulation of the right ventricular outflow tract induced a ventricular arrhythmia that was terminated by cardioversion. The authors attribute the unmasking of Brugada syndrome to lamotrigine.

An implantable cardiac defibrillator was recommended and discussed, but the patient refused further treatment and also refused genetic testing. Neurology was advised to discontinue lamotrigine, which was discontinued after the initial admission, and he is currently receiving levetiracetam. At follow-up 3 months after the initial admission he had no further seizures or syncopal episodes, and ECGs after lamotrigine discontinuation showed normal sinus rhythm with near complete resolution of the J-point elevation and type 1 Brugada pattern.
